question: What is the same-origin policy, and how does CORS let a server explicitly opt in to allowing cross-origin requests?

question: What is a cross-site scripting (XSS) attack, and what are the main techniques for preventing it in a web application?

output encoding/escaping user-supplied content before rendering it as HTML is the primary defense, ensuring injected markup is displayed as literal text rather than executed

most modern frontend frameworks (React, Vue, Angular) escape rendered content by default, which is why explicitly bypassing that default (e.g. dangerouslySetInnerHTML) is specifically flagged as dangerous and needs its own careful sanitization
a Content Security Policy header provides defense-in-depth by restricting which script sources the browser is even allowed to execute, limiting the damage even if an escaping mistake slips through

question: What is a cross-site request forgery (CSRF) attack, and how do anti-CSRF tokens and the SameSite cookie attribute each help prevent it?

question: What does a Content Security Policy (CSP) header do, and how does it help mitigate the impact of an XSS vulnerability even if one exists?

a strict CSP can also disallow inline scripts and eval entirely, closing off common, easy XSS injection vectors that don't require loading an external file at all

question: Walk through the critical rendering path: what steps does a browser take from receiving HTML to actually painting pixels on the screen?

question: What is 'critical CSS' and how does inlining it help improve perceived page load performance?

inlining just the critical CSS directly in the HTML's <head> lets the browser render the above-the-fold content immediately, without waiting on an extra network request for the full stylesheet
the remaining, non-critical CSS is loaded asynchronously afterward, so it doesn't block that initial paint, applying once it arrives for content further down the page

question: What are the three Core Web Vitals metrics (LCP, INP, CLS), and what user-facing experience does each one actually measure?

key_points: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) measures how long it takes for the largest visible content element to finish rendering, roughly capturing when the page feels like it's 'loaded' to the user
Interaction to Next Paint (INP) measures the latency of user interactions throughout the page's lifetime, capturing how responsive the page feels when a user actually clicks, taps, or types

Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures how much visible content unexpectedly shifts position during loading, capturing the frustrating experience of content jumping around as things like images or ads load in

these three together were chosen specifically because they map to distinct, genuinely important dimensions of user experience: loading speed, interactivity, and visual stability, rather than one single overall number

INP replaced the older First Input Delay (FID) metric specifically because FID only measured the delay before the first interaction started processing, while INP measures interaction responsiveness across the entire page lifetime, more representative of real ongoing usage

Interaction to Next Paint measures the latency of user interactions across the page's entire lifetime, capturing how responsive the page genuinely feels whenever a user actually clicks, taps, or types something. Cumulative Layout Shift measures how much visible content unexpectedly shifts position during loading, capturing that frustrating experience of content jumping around unpredictably as things like images or ads finish loading in later than the surrounding text. These three metrics together were deliberately chosen because they each map to a distinct, genuinely important dimension of user experience — loading speed, interactivity, and visual stability — rather than trying to collapse everything into one single overall score. INP specifically replaced the older First Input Delay metric because FID only measured the delay before the very first interaction started being processed, while INP measures interaction responsiveness across the entire page's lifetime, which is a genuinely more representative picture of real, ongoing usage.

question: Compare cache-first and network-first caching strategies for a service worker intercepting requests. When would you use each?

network-first tries the network first, only falling back to the cache if the network request fails, favoring up-to-date content over raw speed, at the cost of waiting on the network when it's available but slow
cache-first suits static assets that rarely change (app shell, versioned bundles), where staleness practically never matters since a new deploy ships new filenames anyway
network-first suits content that genuinely needs to be fresh (like an API response with frequently changing data), where serving stale cached data would actually mislead the user

stale-while-revalidate is a common middle ground: serve the cached response immediately for speed, then fetch an updated version in the background to refresh the cache for next time, without making the current request wait on that background update

question: What's the difference between progressive enhancement and graceful degradation as approaches to building a web page that works across varying levels of browser capability?

key_points: progressive enhancement starts by building a basic, fully functional experience using the most widely-supported features (plain HTML/CSS), then layers on more advanced JavaScript-driven enhancements for browsers that support them

graceful degradation instead starts by building the full, most advanced experience first, then adds fallback handling to keep it from breaking completely on browsers or conditions that lack some capability

progressive enhancement guarantees a genuinely working baseline for every user by construction, since that baseline is what's built first; graceful degradation depends on the developer correctly anticipating every way the advanced experience could fail and building a fallback for each one
progressive enhancement fits naturally with things like ensuring a form still submits via a plain HTML form action even if JavaScript fails to load or execute for any reason

in practice, most modern teams lean toward progressive enhancement for its more reliable baseline guarantee, though graceful degradation is a reasonable pragmatic choice when the target audience's capabilities are well understood and unlikely to vary much

Progressive enhancement guarantees a genuinely working baseline for every single user by construction, since that baseline is literally what gets built first, while graceful degradation depends entirely on the developer correctly anticipating every single way the advanced experience could fail and building an explicit fallback for each one, which is much easier to get wrong or simply miss a case. Progressive enhancement fits naturally with things like making sure a form still submits correctly through a plain HTML form action even if JavaScript fails to load or execute for any reason at all. In practice, most modern teams lean toward progressive enhancement specifically for its more reliable baseline guarantee, though graceful degradation remains a reasonable, pragmatic choice when the target audience's actual capabilities are well understood in advance and unlikely to vary much.

question: How does the native HTML5 Drag and Drop API work, and what events does a draggable element and its drop target need to handle?

a potential drop target must explicitly handle dragover and call event.preventDefault() inside it, since the browser's default behavior otherwise disallows dropping on most elements
the drop target handles the drop event itself, reading the transferred data via event.dataTransfer.getData() and performing whatever action the drop represents

this native API handles the low-level drag lifecycle and cross-window/cross-application dragging, but doesn't provide things like smooth visual reordering animations out of the box, which is why many apps still use a JS library built on top of, or instead of, these raw native events for a polished drag-and-drop UI

The source element handles the dragstart event to set the data actually being transferred, using event.dataTransfer.setData, and optionally handles dragend for any cleanup once the drag operation finishes, successfully or not. question: Why is `requestAnimationFrame` generally preferred over `setTimeout` or `setInterval` for running a JavaScript animation loop?

key_points: requestAnimationFrame schedules a callback to run right before the browser's next repaint, syncing the animation update to the browser's actual rendering cycle rather than an arbitrary fixed time interval

setTimeout/setInterval run on a fixed timer with no awareness of the browser's actual repaint timing, which can cause updates to happen out of sync with what's actually being painted, wasting work or causing visible stutter

the browser automatically pauses requestAnimationFrame callbacks when the tab is in a background/inactive tab, saving battery and CPU, while a naive setTimeout loop would keep firing uselessly in the background

requestAnimationFrame's callback receives a high-resolution timestamp, making it straightforward to calculate frame-accurate, time-based animation progress rather than assuming a fixed, possibly-inaccurate interval actually elapsed

using setTimeout/setInterval for animation can result in a frame rate that doesn't actually match the display's refresh rate, since the fixed interval you chose has no relationship to when the browser is actually about to repaint
reference_solution.sample_answer: requestAnimationFrame schedules a callback to run right before the browser's next actual repaint, syncing the animation update directly to the browser's real rendering cycle, rather than to some arbitrary fixed time interval you happened to choose. setTimeout and setInterval instead run on a fixed timer with absolutely no awareness of the browser's actual repaint timing, which can cause your updates to happen out of sync with what's actually being painted to the screen, wasting work computing frames that never actually get shown, or causing visible stutter. The browser also automatically pauses requestAnimationFrame callbacks entirely when the tab is in a background or inactive tab, which saves battery and CPU, while a naive setTimeout-based loop would just keep firing completely uselessly in the background the whole time. requestAnimationFrame's callback also receives a high-resolution timestamp as an argument, making it straightforward to calculate genuinely frame-accurate, time-based animation progress rather than just assuming a fixed, possibly-inaccurate interval actually elapsed exactly as requested. Using setTimeout or setInterval for animation can end up producing a frame rate that doesn't actually match the display's real refresh rate at all, since the fixed interval you chose has no inherent relationship to when the browser is actually about to repaint next.
